doc.title: Cedar Walton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Dallas memories and the Denver years
title: Charlie Parker sits in with his band in Denver
summary: After a Kenton-Gillespie-Parker concert, Parker came to the club and sat in with Walton's band, playing a couple of tunes then dozing off, with Charlie Burrell on bass; Walton places it between 1952 and 1955.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Did you sit in? Did you play with him?
Yeah. He played with, we played … you know, the band I was in uh, he came up and, "Can I sit in with you fellows?" It was very simple.
So you got to talk about that.
Well, that's …
Not [just?] to mention but just …
Yeah, that's about it. When I was at the piano, you know, was a …
Do you remember what you …

I had been to the concert where he played, you know, which uh, a tour which featured Stan Kenton’s Orchestra, special guest, Dizzy Gillespie. Charlie Parker, Frank Rosolino, Erroll Garner played a set, and it was a very exciting concert. And then uh, oh man, about sixty percent of those people came to the club, includin' Charlie Parker. I don't think Dizzy came, but uh, Charlie did. And uh, he played a couple of tunes and then he proceeded to doze off, you know. He was, asked for a chair. It was a rather high stage and so uh, it was uh …
Do you remember what you played?

Uh, Dancing on the Ceiling. Uh, I remember we played things in C which puts it in uh, A-natural for, for alto, and another one uh, in C, but I can't remember exactly what it was. Diane Reeves is, is, is a bit of a trivia on that. Dianne Reeves uncle, Charlie Burrell, was the bassist in that group, and he also played with the Denver Symphony. He played very good jazz bass. He still does, too. I mean, this amazing coincidence, I think, 'cause when I met uh, Dianne, she told me that she was the niece of Charlie Burrell. I said, "Well, no kiddin'?" I said, "Please give him my regards." So those are the things that …
What was it, stay with Bird further, what impression did his playing have on you?
Oh, it was just a great … being in the presence of a great … you would hear him practicing his, in the back, his …
I'm talkin' 'bout Bird.
Oh, Bird. [laughs] Uh, he ...
He can come too...

No, no, Bird was just a little bit slow that night. Uh, uh, I think he'd consumed a little bit too much scotch and so, it's not … I don't enjoy talkin' about anything except the fact that he set in, and the guy taped it, and I wanted to hear that but he erased it. So I was goin' after him with a chain saw. I said, "Man, how could you erase that?" So it wasn't uh, the true Charlie Parker, uh, since you drew it out of me, Mr. Brower. I didn't want to talk, you know, negatively …
What year was that at the time?
Oh, it was, all those years was the '50s.
Oh man, uh …
I mean, would it be music...near the end so to speak of Parker… would have to be.
[pause] It was between '52 and '55 'cause I came to New York in '55. So it was between those two years.
